capitals.name: Itinerant, Maniapoto country (King Country); no fixed seat

ledger.x: 1858: Pōtatau Te Wherowhero is crowned the first Māori king at Ngāruawāhia.
1863: the invasion of the Waikato begins.

1863: Ngāruawāhia falls. the Kīngitanga capital at Ngāruawāhia was abandoned and then taken by Cameron's troops on 8 December 1863 (closely paraphrased), after Rangiriri on 20-21 November; the king's seat then moves south into Maniapoto country.

1864: the Waikato campaign ends at Ōrākau. Ōrākau was besieged from 31 March and the garrison broke out on 2 April 1864; 'The campaign ended with the retreat of the Kingitanga Māori into the rugged interior of the North Island.'
1864: the Waikato is lost; the Kīngitanga withdraws to the King Country.
1864: the Kīngitanga withdraws into the King Country.

wars.name: Invasion of the Waikato
wars.outcome: British victory: 12 July 1863 crossing of the Mangatāwhiri, Rangiriri 20-21 November 1863, Ngāruawāhia taken 8 December 1863, Te Awamutu 21 February 1864, Ōrākau 31 March-2 April 1864; the Kīngitanga retreated to the King Country and about 486,500 ha of…

certainty.note: A king's proclaimed boundary (Maungatautari), not a surveyed line.

The aukati, a line of pā on the Pūniu River near Kihikihi, was a recognised frontier closed to Europeans 'under threat of death'; the southern and eastern edges (upper Whanganui, Hauhungaroa and Rangitoto Ranges) are approximate.
